notes: Phytopthora:

Phytophthora dieback is a devastating plant disease caused by a soil-borne water mould, Phytophthora cinnamomi, that attacks the roots of susceptible plants, leading to root rot and ultimately plant death
Cause:
Phytophthora dieback is caused by the pathogen Phytophthora cinnamomi, a microscopic water mould that thrives in the soil and plant tissue.
Mechanism:
The pathogen attacks the roots of plants, causing them to rot and die, preventing the plant from taking up water and nutrients.
Impact:
It can cause significant damage to native ecosystems, leading to the death of important plant species and the loss of habitat for animals.
Spread:
The disease spreads through the movement of infested soil, water, and even through the tools and boots of people and animals.
Susceptible plants:
Many native plants, including Banksias, Jarrah trees, and grass trees are susceptible to Phytophthora dieback.
Control & management:
There is no cure for the disease once it is established, and focus is on preventing its spread and mitigating its impact.
No cure, but some treatments:
Phosphite, a non-hazardous and biodegradable fungicide, is currently the only chemical treatment available for Phytophthora dieback.
Threats to native species and ecosystems:
The disease has resulted in a major decline of native vegetation across the south-west region of Western Australia, Tasmania, and Queensland.
Myrtle Rust
Myrtle rust is a disease caused by the exotic fungus Austropuccinia psidii (formerly Puccinia psidii, initially identified as Uredo rangelii).

Myrtle rust threatens trees and shrubs in the Myrtaceae family of plants. Myrtaceae is the largest plant family in Australia and includes native plants such as tea tree (Melaleuca spp.) and eucalypts (Eucalyptus spp., Angophora spp., and Corymbia spp.).
The disease can:
cause deformed leaves
stunt growth
reduce fertility
cause heavy defoliation of branches
kill plants.
There are at least 15 rainforest tree species at risk of extinction in the wild due to myrtle rust infection.

Currently, only one strain of myrtle rust exists within Australia. However, other strains are present overseas. These close relatives of myrtle rust could have devastating impacts on Australian plants if they were to enter Australia.
This is why biosecurity measures are essential to ensure other strains of myrtle rust do not enter Australia in the future.
Preventing the spread
It is important to understand what you can do to minimise the human-driven spread of myrtle rust.
You can help prevent spread by:
regularly cleaning gardening tools and equipment
inspecting your garden regularly for signs of myrtle rust
ensuring you check for signs of myrtle rust when purchasing plants
not moving or collecting infected plants or plant material. If you suspect a plant in your garden has myrtle rust, report it to your state or territory biosecurity authority
washing clothes you wear in nurseries, parks or bushland before entering other areas
treating myrtle rust in your home garden or plant nursery as appropriate
consulting your local garden centre on approved fungicides for treating myrtle rust.
